newsitem.title: JAPAN: G7 may agree at meeting that yen too weak - Gyohten.
newsitem.headline: G7 may agree at meeting that yen too weak - Gyohten.

text.p: The Group of Seven (G7) nations may agree at their meeting this weekend that the yen's recent weakening is excessive, said Toyoo Gyohten, a former key Japanese finance ministry official.
He added that the United States is strongly concerned about its rising trade deficit with Japan.
"It is true that the United States is strongly concerned about the rising trend of Japan's trade surplus with the U.S.," Gyohten told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.

But Gyohten, a senior advisor to the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd and a former Japanese vice minister of finance for international affairs, added that he did not expect Japan's trade surplus to increase substantially anytime soon.
"I don't think a day will come soon when the ratio of Japan's (current account) surplus to GDP will exceed three percent," he said.

The former finance ministry official said the rise in the surplus was due to the depreciation of the yen over the last two years, adding that if the current yen weakness continues the surplus will increase as well.
Gyohten said that the current level of the dollar at 125 yen was clearly excessive and that the appropriate level was between 100 and 110 yen.
Gyohten, who as a finance ministry official in the past took part in G7 meetings, said the G7 nations may come to an agreement at the meeting this weekend that the yen has fallen too far.
"One realistic scenario is for the nations to make it clear that the yen's weakness is excessive," he said.
He added that if the monetary authorities are able to show that they share the same views on currencies, that will have an effect on the market.
But he said the question still remained as to whether the United States will agree to correct the yen's weakness.

Gyohten said Washington is fearful that by doing so, it may precipitate a prolonged decline in the dollar, bringing about a drop in capital flows to the United States and leading to a rise in long-term interest rates and a fall in stock prices.
"The U.S. position is a delicate one. It's not desirable for Japan's surplus to rise, but on the other hand, they're worried about a resurgence of a weak dollar," Gyohten said.
He also said there were views among Japanese authorities that the weakness of the yen, at around 126 yen to the dollar, was having positive effects on some industries.
He added that if the United States came to an agreement with Japan and conducted coordinated intervention, it would effectively correct the yen's excessive weakness.
"The market is nervous about (the yen's weakness). Regardless of the timing, large-scale coordinated intervention by the U.S. and Japan would be highly effective," Gyohten said.
On the Japanese economy, Gyohten said the recovery was now able to withstand an interest rate rise.
"I think it's about time we start reviewing current interest rates. The Japanese economic recovery is not so weak that it will all of a sudden collapse if there is a rate rise," he said.
He added that by autumn the recovery will become more evident. -- Tokyo Policy Desk +81-3-5473-3710
